head.ce:title: Divergent total synthesis of indolizidine-, quinolizidine-, and decahydroquinoline-type poison-frog alkaloids

ce:affiliation.ce:textfn: Faculty of Engineering, University of Toyama, Toyama, Japan
ce:affiliation.ce:source-text: Faculty of Engineering, University of Toyama, Toyama 930-8555, Japan

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The skin extracts of Neotropical poison-frogs contain a variety of lipophilic alkaloids, and over 800 alkaloids representing >20 structural classes have been isolated or detected to date. Pumiliotoxins (PTXs) and decahydroquinolines (DHQs) are the major classes of poison-frog alkaloids, and their structural diversity and pharmacological activity have stimulated considerable interest in their chemical synthesis by several groups. However, no divergent synthesis of PTXs and DHQs have been reported so far. We have achieved the divergent total synthesis of these alkaloids and were able to establish that chiral building blocks (2R,3S)-ethyl 1-allyl-3-hydroxy-6-oxopiperidine-2-carboxylate (−)-1 and (2R,6S)-1-benzyl 2-methyl 6-(acetoxymethyl)piperidine-1,2-dicarboxylate 75 are extremely useful and versatile for the synthesis of natural products, especially indolizidine, quinolizidine, and decahydroquinoline alkaloids.

ce:section.ce:para: Nitrogen-containing heterocycles, such as indolizidine, quinolizidine, and decahydroquinoline, have unique structural features and interesting biological activities (Fig. 1).

Consequently, considerable efforts have been devoted to the development of constructing these ring systems in a highly stereocontrolled manner.1 To date, over 800 lipophilic alkaloids representing >20 structural classes have been detected from the skin extracts of poison-frogs.2 Remarkable examples of poison-frog alkaloids are (−)-batrachotoxin and (−)-epibatidine (Fig. 2). (−)-Batrachotoxin is known to be the most potent toxic component of land organism, and (−)-epibatidine exhibits nicotinic agonistic activity, which has greatly influenced the study of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs).3

Many of these alkaloids are expected to exhibit significant biological activities in the nervous system such as nAChRs and have attracted attention as valuable drug discovery resources. However, methods for chemical synthesis of poison-frog alkaloids are needed to investigate the biological activities of these interesting alkaloids as only trace amounts can be obtained from skin extracts. Pumiliotoxins (PTXs) and decahydroquinolines (DHQs) are the major classes of poison-frog alkaloids, and their structural diversity and pharmacological activity have stimulated considerable interest in their chemical synthesis by several groups. Some of the proposed structures for PTXs and DHQs are tentative, while others have been rigorously established by MS, FT-IR, NMR spectra, and/or synthesis (Fig. 3).

At present, over 30 alkaloids are considered to be PTXs and over 60 alkaloids belong to various congeners, such as homopumiliotoxins (hPTXs) having a quinolizidine ring system instead of indolizidine, 8-deoxy-pumiliotoxins (8-deoxy-PTXs), 9-deoxy-homopumiliotoxins (9-deoxy-hPTXs), 8-desmethyl-pumiliotoxins (8-desmethyl-PTXs), and 9-desmethyl-homopumiliotoxins (9-desmethyl-hPTXs) (Fig. 4).

Some PTXs have been reported to show interesting biological activities, such as the activation of sodium and calcium channels.4 However, the PTXs and their congeners have been detected in minute amounts from the skin extracts of poison-frogs, and only a few alkaloids, such as PTX 251D, have been isolated. The structures of PTX 251D,5 8-deoxy-PTX 251H,6 and hPTX 223G7 were established by X-ray crystallography or NMR analysis, while those of the other PTXs and their congeners are tentative (Fig. 5). Additionally, synthesis and associated synthetic attempts have been reported in only a few examples, such as PTX 251D,8 and no reports on the exhaustive and effective synthesis of PTXs and their congeners exist.

Therefore, it is extremely important to secure substantial amounts of PTXs and their congeners by organic synthesis to explore the biological activities of this class of alkaloids. As part of a larger research program directed at studying the synthesis of poison-frog alkaloids, we have attempted the divergent synthesis of PTX 209F, hPTX 223G, 8-deoxy-PTX 193H, 9-deoxy-hPTX 207O, 8-desmethyl-PTX 195, and 9-desmethyl-hPTX 209H from the common chiral building block (2R,3S)-ethyl 1-allyl-3-hydroxy-6-oxopiperidine-2-carboxylate (−)-1 prepared from allylamine (Fig. 6).

Among PTXs, we first attempted to synthesize 8-deoxy-PTX 193H and 9-deoxy-hPTX 207O. The synthesis began with β-keto ester (±)-2, which was prepared in 3 steps including Dieckmann condensation from allylamine.9 Reduction of (±)-2 with NaBH4 yielded only a small amount of the desired racemic alcohol (±)-1 (<20% yield) and a complex mixture containing undesired diol, which was reduced ketone and ester moiety, as a major product. On the other hand, bakers' yeast reduction of (±)-2 under nonfermenting conditions gave rise to the enantiopure alcohol (−)-1 in good yield and high optical purity (>98% ee).10 Treatment of (−)-1 with bis(2-methoxyethyl) azodicarboxylate (BMEAD) and Ph3P provided the enaminoester (±)-3, which was subjected to copper-mediated 1,4-addition of methyllithium, followed by reduction of the resulting adduct with Super-Hydride® to afford the primary alcohol (±)-4 in high yield as a single isomer (Scheme 1).

To obtain both enantiomers of (+)- and (−)-4, lipase-mediated kinetic resolution of (±)-4 with lipase PL and vinyl acetate in t-BuOMe was conducted and resulted in the acetate 5 in 55% yield with 58% ee, and the alcohol (−)-4 in 36% yield with >98% ee, respectively. Since the ee of the acetate 5 from the initial resolution was not sufficient for further transformation, the acetate 5 was hydrolyzed to the corresponding alcohol 4′, which was then subjected to the second kinetic resolution under the same reaction conditions to obtain the acetate (+)-5. Hydrolysis of the enantiopure acetate (+)-5 with NaOH gave the enantiopure alcohol (+)-4 with 98% ee, as shown in Scheme 2. The use of other lipases (Meito SL, Novozym 435, etc.) and solvents (benzene, EtOAc, acetone, CH2Cl2, MeCN, Me2O, Et2O, i-Pr2O, THF, 1,4-dioxane, etc.) were found to significantly reduce the optical purity of (+)- and (−)-4.

Once both enantiomers of 4 were obtained, we performed a Swern oxidation of (−)-4, which was followed by a Wittig reaction of the resulting aldehyde. The Wittig reaction provided the diene (−)-6, which was converted to the tetrahydroindolizin-5-one (−)-7 by ring-closing metathesis using a 2nd generation Grubbs catalyst. Hydrogenation of (−)-7 over 10% Pd/C resulted in the indolizidinone (−)-8. The absolute stereochemistry of (−)-8 was determined to be 5R, 6R by comparing the optical rotation between our synthetic (−)-8 with known (+)-8.11 Indolizidinone (−)-8 was subjected to an aldol condensation with isobutyraldehyde to afford the aldol adduct 9. Stereospecific syn-elimination of 9 using DCC/CuCl [8b] afforded the desired (Z)-olefin (−)-10 with no (E)-olefin. Finally, a reduction of the lactam moiety of (−)-10 using AlH3, resulted in the formation of (−)-8-deoxy-PTX 193H (Scheme 3). The 1H and 13C NMR spectra of our synthetic (−)-8-deoxy-PTX 193H were in good accordance with data from the literature, however the optical rotation was opposite.12
The enantiomer (+)-8-deoxy-PTX 193H was also synthesized from (+)-4 in the same manner, as shown in Scheme 4.

Furthermore, both enantiomers of (+)- and (−)-9-deoxy-hPTX 207O were also synthesized from the alcohols (−)- and (+)-4. The alcohol (−)-4 was converted to the iodide (+)-11, which was subjected to a cross-coupling reaction with vinylmagnesium chloride in the presence of HMPA and P(OEt)313 to afford the diallylpiperidone (−)-12 in 62% yield, together with the undesired ring-opened amide 13 in 22% yield, respectively. The ring-closing methathesis reaction of (−)-12 using a 2nd generation Grubbs catalyst, followed by hydrogenation of the resulting olefin (−)-14, provided the corresponding quinolizidinone, which was subjected to an aldol condensation to afford the aldol adduct 15 (Scheme 5).

Stereospecific syn-elimination of 15 using DCC/CuCl gave the undesired (E)-olefin (+)-16 in 81% yield, while anti-elimination [8b] by mesylation of 15, followed by treatment of the resulting mesylate with KOH, provided the desired (Z)-olefin (+)-17 in 70% yield in 2 steps. The double bond geometry in (+)-16 and (+)-17 was determined based on the chemical shift of the vinyl proton using 1H NMR spectra. The vinyl proton of the (Z)-olefin (+)-17 was detected in a high magnetic field (δ 5.45ppm), while that of the (E)-olefin (+)-16 was present in a low magnetic field (δ 6.56ppm) due to the anisotropy of the amide‑carbonyl group.14 It was noteworthy that the aldol adducts for indolizidine ring system and quinolizidine ring system were opposite. Finally, reduction of (+)-17 by treatment with AlH3 resulted in the formation of (+)-deoxy-hPTX 207O (Scheme 6).
The enantiomer (−)-deoxy-hPTX 207O was also synthesized from (+)-4 in the same manner, as shown in Scheme 7.

We prepared the versatile lactam-type chiral building block (−)-1 for the divergent synthesis of PTXs and their congeners. With this chiral building block (−)-1, we achieved the enantioselective synthesis of 8-deoxy-PTX 193H and 9-deoxy-hPTX 207O from the enantiopure alcohol (+)- and (−)-4, which were prepared by lipase-mediated kinetic resolution of racemic (±)-4 (Fig. 7).15

As the next target starting from (−)-1, we set up the synthesis of desmethyl-PTX-type poison-frog alkaloids. Protection of the hydroxyl group in (−)-1 with MOMCl and DIPEA provided the corresponding MOM ether, which was reduced with Super-Hydride® to afford the primary alcohol (−)-18 in good yield. Swern oxidation of (−)-18 followed by a Wittig reaction of the resulting aldehyde gave the diene (−)-19 in 85% yield over two steps. The ring-closing metathesis reaction of (−)-19 using a 2nd generation Grubbs catalyst and then hydrogenation of the resulting olefin (−)-20 over 10% Pd/C gave the corresponding indolizidinone, which was subjected to an aldol condensation with isobutyraldehyde to afford a mixture of the aldol adducts 21a and 21b. The mixture of 21a and 21b was easily separated by column chromatography (Scheme 8).

Stereospecific syn-elimination of 21a using DCC and CuCl [8b] gave the desired (Z)-olefin (−)-22 as a single isomer. The double bond geometry in (−)-22 was determined to be Z by the chemical shift of the vinyl proton (δ 5.59ppm). Deprotection of the MOM protecting group in (−)-22 followed by treatment of the resulting alcohol with LiAlH4 and AlCl3 furnished (−)-8-desmethyl-PTX 195. Syn-elimination of 21b exclusively provided the undesired (E)-olefin (−)-23, whose structure was also determined by the chemical shift of the vinyl proton (δ 6.74ppm) because of the anisotropy of the lactam‑carbonyl group (Scheme 9).14 From the above results, the structure of the aldol adduct 21a should be the syn-isomer and 21b should be the anti-isomer, respectively. By comparison, anti-elimination of 21b by mesylation followed by treatment of the resulting mesylate with KOH gave the desired (Z)-olefin (−)-22 in 33% yield over two steps, along with the undesired (E)-olefin (−)-23 in 66% yield over two steps. To account for the unexpected results from the anti-elimination reaction of 21b, we proposed two pathways leading to the desired (Z)-olefin and (E)-olefin as shown in Fig. 8. The direct anti-elimination of mesylate A, derived from 21b, resulted in the formation of the desired (Z)-olefin (−)-22 (path A), while the elimination of A via the lactam-enolate C generated the undesired (E)-olefin (−)-23 (path B). Additionally, the C conformer is favored relative to B because of the A(1,3)-strain between the lactam-enolate moiety and the isopropyl group. On the basis of the result that the ratio of the (Z)-olefin (−)-22 to the (E)-olefin (−)-23 was 1:2, path B is more likely to occur than path A.

Furthermore, 9-desmethyl-hPTX poison-frog alkaloid was synthesized from the common alcohol (−)-18. We performed Swern oxidation of (−)-18 and then the Horner-Wadsworth-Emmons (HWE) reaction of the resulting aldehyde. The HWE reaction provided the α,β-unsaturated ester (−)-24, which was converted to the saturated methyl ester (−)-25 by a one-electron reduction using a Mg/MeOH system. The 1,4-reduction of (−)-24 was also attempted, but a complex mixture was obtained, and the desired product could not be obtained. Treatment of (−)-25 with Super-Hydride® resulted in the alcohol (−)-26, which was transformed into the diallylpiperidone (−)-27 in good yield by the Nishizawa-Grieco method.16 The ring-closing metathesis reaction of (−)-27 provided the olefin (+)-28 followed by hydrogenation over 10% Pd/C to afford the corresponding quinolizidinone, which was subjected to an aldol condensation to give rise to the aldol adduct 29, as shown in Scheme 10.

Unfortunately, stereospecific syn-elimination of 29 gave the undesired (E)-olefin (+)-30 as a single isomer. The double bond geometry of (+)-30 was determined to be E because of the detection of the vinyl proton at low magnetic field (δ 6.71ppm). From the above results, the structure of 29 should be the anti-isomer. Therefore, to obtain the desired (Z)-olefin (+)-31, we conducted the anti-elimination by two steps of mesylation followed by the treatment of the resulting mesylate with KOH. The result of the anti-elimination of 29 was quite similar to that of 21b, and both (+)-30 and (+)-31 were obtained in 54% and 27% yield, respectively. The vinyl proton of (+)-31 was detected at high magnetic field (δ 5.51ppm) to prove the Z-geometry. After separation of (+)-30 and (+)-31 by column chromatography, (+)-31 was transformed into (−)-9-desmethyl-hPTX 209H by the deprotection of the MOM protecting group followed by treatment of the resulting alcohol with AlH3 (Scheme 11).

Next, we examined the synthesis of PTX 209F from the common diene (−)-19 derived from (−)-1. To introduce the methyl group at the 5-position, deprotection of the MOM protecting group in (−)-19 followed by the oxidation of the resulting alcohol provided the corresponding ketone, which was treated with MeMgBr to give rise to the tertiary alcohol (−)-32 as a single isomer. The ring-closing metathesis reaction of (−)-32 using a 2nd generation Grubbs catalyst and then hydrogenation of the resulting olefin (−)-33 gave the indolizidinone (−)-34. The relative stereochemistry of (−)-34 was determined by comparing the 1H NMR spectra and optical rotation between our synthetic (−)-34 with known (−)-34 [8b]. Indolizidinone (−)-34 was subjected to an aldol condensation with isobutyraldehyde to afford the aldol adducts 35a and 35b (Scheme 12).

The stereoselectivity of the Grignard reaction of ketone 19′ prepared from (−)-19 may be attributed to the steric hindrance as shown in Fig. 9 by which the Grignard reaction will occur from the less hindered and stereoelectronically favored β-face. This will fix the conformation not in D but in E because of the A(1,2)-strain between the N-allyl group and the α-vinyl group17 to exclusively afford (−)-32.

Stereospecific syn-elimination of 35a using DCC/CuCl afforded the desired (Z)-olefin (−)-36 with no (E)-olefin. By comparison, syn-elimination of 35b provided (−)-37, the only undesired (E)-olefin. From the above result, we performed the anti-elimination of 35b to obtain the desired (Z)-olefin (−)-36 in 39% over two steps together with the undesired (E)-olefin (−)-37 in 53% over two steps. Finally, a reduction of the lactam moiety of (−)-36 furnished (−)-PTX 209F. The 1H NMR and optical rotation of our synthetic (−)-PTX 209F were in good accordance with data from the literature (Scheme 13) [8h].

Finally, we investigated the synthesis of hPTX 223G to achieve the divergent synthesis of PTX-type poison-frog alkaloids. Deprotection of the MOM protecting group in (−)-27 and then the treatment with Dess-Martin periodinane (DMP) of the resulting alcohol gave the corresponding ketone, which was transformed into the tertiary alcohol (−)-38. The stereoselectivity of the above Grignard reaction was the same as that shown in Fig. 9. The ring-closing metathesis reaction of (−)-38 followed by hydrogenation of the resulting olefin (−)-39 afforded the quinolizidinone (+)-40. The relative stereochemistry of (+)-40 was determined by comparing the 1H NMR spectra and optical rotation between our synthetic (+)-40 with known (−)-40 ((+)-40: [α]D26+24.7 (c 0.25, CHCl3) [lit. (−)-40: [α]D20–20.4 (c 0.50, CHCl3)]).18 Quinolizidinone (+)-40 is the key intermediate for the total synthesis of hPTX 223G as described by L. Silva.14 Thus, we had achieved the formal synthesis of (+)-hPTX 223G, as shown in Scheme 14.

In summary, we have achieved the divergent total synthesis of PTX 209F, hPTX 223G, 8-deoxy-PTX 193H, 9-deoxy-hPTX 207O, 8-desmethyl-PTX 195, and 9-desmethyl-hPTX 209H from the common chiral building block (−)-1.19 It is noteworthy that (2R,3S)-ethyl 1-allyl-3-hydroxy-6-oxopiperidine-2-carboxylate (−)-1 is extremely useful and versatile for the synthesis of natural products, especially indolizidine and quinolizidine alkaloids.

DHQs are a relatively large subgroup of poison-frog alkaloids, and over 50 types have been detected, such as the cis-, 2-epi-cis-, and trans-isomers. Considering the relationship of the hydrogens in the fused ring of the DHQ skeleton, the 4a-epi-cis isomer, an unnatural form, may also be classified as a DHQ. However, no divergent synthesis of this class of alkaloids has been reported, and pharmacological studies on these alkaloids have not been investigated in detail. In addition, the relative and absolute configurations of some of these alkaloids have not been determined. Therefore, the establishment of a divergent synthetic strategy for these alkaloids is important for both structural determination and detailed biological evaluations (Fig. 10).

Among DHQs, DHQ cis-195A is the parent member of this class that was originally isolated from a Panamanian population of Oophaga (Dendrobates) pumilio in 1969.20 The structure and absolute configuration of DHQ cis-195A were determined by X-ray crystallography, and several total syntheses have also been reported for this compound.21 DHQ cis-211A was isolated from skin extracts of the same species of poison frog in 1987 [22]. However, no total synthesis of DHQ cis-211A has been reported and its absolute configuration remains unknown to date. First, we examined the total synthesis of DHQ ent-cis-195A and DHQ cis-211A. The synthesis of DHQ cis-211A also enabled the determination of its absolute configuration (Fig. 11).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Total synthesis of DHQ ent-cis-195A and DHQ cis-211A
ce:section.ce:para: Our research group has been working on synthetic studies of various natural products using stereoselective Michael-type conjugate addition reactions. This strategy is based on conformational control that is governed by the allylic strain and the stereoelectronic effect. The conjugate addition reaction to acyclic urethane 41 and cyclic urethane 42 with organocopper reagents afforded the corresponding trisubstituted piperidine core systems 43 and 44 in good yields as single stereoisomers, respectively (Fig. 12) [23].

The high stereoselectivity of the above reaction can be explained as shown in Fig. 13. The attack of the organocopper species should be preferred from the stereoelectronically favored α-axial orientation of conformation 41A to form the adduct 43. The alternative conformation 41B is disfavored because of the A(1,3) strain between the methyl urethane and the alkyl (R) group [24]. Similarly in the case of 42, the nucleophilic attack of the organocopper reagent is expected to occur from the more stereoelectronically favorable β-face on 42A to give the adduct 44.
We achieved the total synthesis of DHQ-type poison-frog alkaloids DHQ ent-cis-195A and DHQ cis-211A by using a stereoselective Michael-type conjugate addition reaction as the key step.

The synthesis began with the known allyl derivative 45, which was easily prepared over four steps from D-pipecolic acid [25]. Hydrogenation of 45 provided the ester 46, which was converted to enaminoester 48 via thiophenyl derivative 47. The Michael-type conjugate addition reaction to 48 gave adduct 49 as a single isomer in excellent yield [23d]. The ester moiety of 49 was elongated by the Arndt-Eistert reaction sequence to afford the homologated ester 50, which was transformed into the methyl ketone 52 via the corresponding Weinreb amide 51. Lemieux-Johnson oxidation of 52 provided the aldehyde 53, which was subjected to cyclization by treatment with DBU in refluxing benzene to yield the cis-fused enone 54 [23d] without generating the trans-fused enone 55. Selective formation of 54 was explained by the preferential formation of conformer F in the starting material 53 owing to the A(1,3) strain. Thus, epimerization at the 3-position of 53 occurred first, and then cyclization proceeded to provide the enone 54 as shown in Fig. 14. With cis-fused enone 54 in hand, the stage was set for the divergent synthesis of ent-cis-195A and cis-211A. The conjugate addition reaction to 54 with Me2CuLi followed by treatment of the resulting enolate with Comins' triflating agent [26] afforded the common and key intermediate enol triflate 56 (Scheme 15).

Finally, global hydrogenation of 56 and deprotection of the methyl carbamate moiety in 57 using TMSI in CHCl3 at 50°C provided DHQ ent-cis-195A as shown in Scheme 16. The 1H and 13C NMR spectra of synthetic DHQ ent-cis-195A were in good agreement with those reported in the literature.21r

Next, we investigated the total synthesis of DHQ cis-211A from enol triflate 56, which was converted to olefin 58 by palladium-catalyzed reduction. Epoxidation of 58 by mCPBA proceeded smoothly to give the epoxide 59; unfortunately, as a 1:1 mixture of epoxide 59. Hydroboration of 58 under several conditions provided the alcohol 60 and the mixture of alcohols 61 and 62, as shown in Table 1. The structure of 60 was determined by NOESY. The NOESY experiments of 60 revealed a syn relationship between the methyl group at C-5 and H-6 based on the NOESY correlations from H3-5 to H-6. However, the separation of 61 and 62 was difficult at this stage. For completion of the synthesis of DHQ cis-211A, inversion of the hydroxyl group in 60 was necessary. For this purpose, we subjected 60 to the Mitsunobu reaction; however, all attempts failed and resulted in the recovery of 60. Next, we examined hydroxyl inversion of 60 via ketone 64. Any oxidations of 60 using Swern oxidation condition ((COCl)2, DMSO, Et3N), a SO3-pyridine complex, PCC, PDC, DMP, or TPAP were not successful, and the starting material was recovered. Only oxidation using AZADOL® [27] proceeded smoothly to yield the desired ketone 64 in good yield. In addition, the AZADOL® oxidation of the mixture of 61 and 62 afforded the ketones 64 and 65 in 34% and 66% yield, respectively, which could be easily separated by column chromatography. Thus, we succeeded in obtaining the ketone 64 from 58 in 64% (49% +15%) overall yield as shown in Scheme 17. The conformation of ketone 64 is depicted in H. The reduction of 64 from the concave face was needed to obtain the desired alcohol 61. We expected that the reduction of 64 would proceed from the concave face, as shown in H, because of the steric hindrance of the α-axial methyl group. However, the use of a small reducing agent like NaBH4 or LiAlH4 reduced 64 from the convex face to afford 62 as the sole product. To secure the reduction from the concave face, we tried the large reducing agent l-Selectride®, however, the reduction did not proceed and only ketone 64 was recovered. Fortunately, Super-Hydride®, a moderately sized reducing agent, was the best match for this substrate, and the reduction proceeded from the concave face to provide the desired alcohol 61 as the major product (61:60=9:1). The final deprotection of the urethane moiety in 61 was also troublesome. First, we applied the same reaction conditions used for DHQ ent-cis-195A (TMSI in refluxing CHCl3) to cleave the methyl carbamate; however, the reaction did not proceed. Then, other reaction conditions, such as the use of n-PrSLi/HMPA or KOH/i-PrOH in a sealed tube at 130°C resulted in the recovery of the starting material. Finally, we used TMSI in refluxing MeCN, and the reaction proceeded cleanly to yield DHQ cis-211A, as shown in Scheme 17.

The 1H and 13C NMR spectra of synthetic cis-211A were in good agreement with the reported values [22]. The absolute stereochemistry of natural DHQ cis-211A was determined unambiguously by the present synthesis to be 2R, 4aR, 5R, 6S, and 8aS by comparison of the optical rotation of synthetic DHQ cis-211A ([α]D25–11.5 (c 0.20, CHCl3)) with the reported value ([α]D−11.7 (c 1.00, CHCl3)) [22]. Interestingly, DHQ cis-195A and DHQ cis-211A were both isolated from the same poison frog, Oophaga (Dendrobates) pumilio (Dendrobatidae) from Panama; however, the absolute stereochemistry of the parent decahydroquinoline nuclei of DHQ cis-195A is opposite to that of DHQ cis-211A.

To further investigate the effect of the stereochemistry of the hydroxyl group at the 6-position on the inhibitory activity against nAChRs, we also synthesized DHQ 6-epi-211A by deprotection of the methoxycarbonyl group in 60 as shown in Scheme 18.

Since many poison-frog alkaloids are expected to exhibit significant biological activities in the nervous system, such as nAChRs, we evaluated the synthesized DHQ ent-cis-195A, DHQ cis-211A, and DHQ 6-epi-211A against nAChRs. nAChRs are ligand-gated cation channels [28]. Homomeric α7- and heteromeric α4β2-pentamers are the major subtypes of nicotinic receptors found in the central nervous system [29]. It has been reported that DHQ cis-195A, a natural cis-DHQ alkaloid (formerly referred to as Pumiliotoxin C) blocks ganglionic nAChRs in pheochromocytoma PC12 cells [30], and that the synthetic analog DHQ ent-cis-195A is more potent than DHQ cis-195A at inhibiting nicotinic receptor activity [31]. Here, we examined the effects of DHQ ent-cis-195A, DHQ cis-211A, and DHQ 6-epi-211A on α7- and α4β2-nAChRs ectopically expressed in Xenopus oocytes. If the criterion for partial inhibition by an alkaloid is defined as a≥20% decrease in the peak amplitude of ACh-elicited currents, then DHQ ent-cis-195A (1–10μM) showed no apparent inhibitory effects on α7- and α4β2-receptor-mediated currents (Fig. 15A and B). DHQ cis-211A and DHQ 6-epi-211A at 10μM partially inhibited α7-receptor-mediated currents by 38% and 31%, respectively, while both alkaloids at 10μM showed negligible effects on α4β2-receptor-mediated currents (Fig. 15C–F). Analysis of their structure-activity relationship suggested that the 6-hydroxy moiety of DHQ cis-211A and DHQ 6-epi-211A might contribute to the partial blockade of α7-nAChRs. The ligand-binding assays showed that none of these alkaloids affected [3H]nicotine and [3H]methyllycaconitine binding to rat whole brain membranes. Therefore, DHQ cis-211A and DHQ 6-epi-211A were believed to act as noncompetitive blockers of α7-nAChRs, although they were less potent and not as highly selective.

Neuronal nAChRs play a role in cerebral and retinal physiology. The blood-brain barrier (BBB) and inner blood-retinal barrier (BRB) directly segregate the brain and retina, respectively, from the circulating blood. It has been reported that putative nicotine- and verapamil-sensitive cationic drug transport systems at the BBB and inner BRB, respectively, are involved in the facilitative distribution of their substrates to the central nervous system [32]. To evaluate the recognition of DHQ ent-cis-195A and DHQ cis-211A as substrates for these cationic drug transport systems, we performed an inhibition study using conditionally-immortalized rat BBB and inner BRB model cells, known as TR-BBB13 and TR-iBRB2 cells [33]. As shown in Table 2, DHQ ent-cis-195A exhibited an inhibitory effect on [3H]nicotine transport into TR-BBB13 cells and [3H]verapamil transport into TR-iBRB2 cells by more than 40%. In addition, the presence of DHQ cis-211A significantly attenuated [3H]nicotine and [3H]verapamil up-take by TR-BBB13 and TR-iBRB2 cells, respectively, by at least 29%. These results suggest that DHQ ent-cis-195A and DHQ cis-211A are recognized by the cationic drug transport systems at the BBB and inner BRB. It is possible that these derivatives reach the brain and retina via the cationic drug transport systems and show neuronal effects in the CNS.

[3H]Nicotine uptake (0.1μCi/well, 6.0nM) by TR-BBB13 cells was measured at 37°C for 10s in the absence (control) or presence of test compounds at 200μM with 1.0% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). Similarly, [3H]verapamil uptake by TR-iBRB2 cells was performed at 37°C for 3min. Each value represents the mean±standard error of the mean S.E.M. (n=3–6). *P<0.01, significantly different from the control in Dunnett's test.

In summary, we achieved the total synthesis of DHQ ent-cis-195A and DHQ cis-211A in a divergent process from the key and common intermediate enol triflate 56. The absolute stereochemistry of natural DHQ cis-211A was determined to be 2R, 4aR, 5R, 6S, and 8aS by comparison with the data obtained from our total synthesis. The inhibitory effects of DHQ ent-cis-195A, DHQ cis-211A, and DHQ 6-epi-211A on nAChRs were also investigated. The results showed that DHQ cis-211A and DHQ 6-epi-211A had better inhibitory effects on the α7-receptor than that of DHQ ent-cis-195A, and none of the compounds showed inhibitory effects on the α4β2-receptor at the same concentration. These results suggested that DHQ cis-211A and DHQ 6-epi-211A could be applied as important tools for studying the brain and nervous system. More interestingly, the absolute configuration of the DHQ nuclei of DHQ cis-211A was a mirror image of that of DHQ cis-195A, even though both alkaloids were isolated from Oophaga (Dendrobates) pumilio from Panama.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Divergent total synthesis of DHQ-type poison-frog alkaloids
ce:section.ce:para: We have achieved the total synthesis of DHQ ent-cis-195A and DHQ cis-211A bearing the cis-DHQ skeleton. In nature, DHQ-type poison-frog alkaloids are not only cis-isomer, but also 4a-epi-cis-, 2-epi-cis-, and trans-isomers, as shown in Fig. 10. However, there have been no reports on the divergent total synthesis of the all isomers of DHQ-type poison-frog alkaloids. We aimed to achieve the divergent total synthesis of all DHQ-type poison-frog alkaloids of cis-, 4a-epi-cis-, 2-epi-cis-, and trans-isomers using the stereoselective Michael-type conjugate addition reaction to urethane 41 and cyclic urethane 42 shown in Fig. 12 as key reactions. In addition, we have been conducting synthetic studies of indolizidines, quinolizidines, tricyclic alkaloids, and their derivatives and evaluated their activities toward nAChRs. From these results, we determined that the derivatives bearing a seven‑carbon chain at the α-position of the nitrogen atom on the piperidine nucleus showed selective and remarkable inhibitory activities against nAChRs [34]. Based on the above findings, we also considered the synthesis of DHQ derivatives bearing a seven‑carbon chain at the α-position of the nitrogen atom on the piperidine.

To comprehensively synthesize these DHQ alkaloids, we designed the synthetic strategy as shown in Scheme 19. Chiral acetate 66 was used as the starting material and was converted to the urethane 67 and oxazolidinone 42 in several steps. Next, a stereoselective Michael-type conjugate addition reaction was applied as the key reaction to urethane 67 and oxazolidinone 42 to give the adducts 68 and 69 as single stereoisomers, respectively. Enones 70 and 71 were synthesized from the adduct 68 in several steps involving an intramolecular aldol cyclization with epimerization and ring-closing metathesis using 2nd generation Grubbs catalyst, respectively. By comparison, enones 72 and 73 were derived from adduct 69 via an intramolecular aldol-type cyclization with epimerization and a ring-closing metathesis reaction after cleavage of the oxazolidinone ring, respectively. Finally, the divergent synthesis of the DHQ-type poison-frog alkaloids was achieved by the stereoselective introduction of any alkyl group to the enones 70, 71, 72, and 73 at the late stage of the synthesis.

First, we examined the synthesis of the cis-isomer as shown generally in Scheme 20. The known chiral acetate 74 was synthesized from 2,6-pyridinedicarboxylic acid according to the literature [35]. Two-step oxidation of 74 followed by treatment of the resulting carboxylic acid with CH2N2 provided the ester 75. Removal of the acetyl group in 75 and then deprotection of the benzyloxy carbonyl (Cbz) group using Pearlman's catalyst gave the corresponding piperidine, which was treated with ClCO2Me to afford the corresponding urethane. The urethane was converted to an olefin bearing a three- or seven‑carbon chain in two steps, which was then hydrogenated over 10% Pd/C to yield the reductants 76a–b in moderate yield over six steps from 75. Thiophenylation of 76a–b followed by oxidation of the resulting S-phenyl derivatives 77a–b using mCPBA gave the enaminoesters 78a–b, which were subjected to the stereoselective Michael-type conjugate addition reaction to afford the adducts 79a–b as single stereoisomers in good yields. The esters 79a–b were converted to the homologated esters 80a–b by the Arndt-Eistert synthesis, which were transformed into the methyl ketones 82a–b via the corresponding Weinreb amides 81a–b. Oxidative cleavage of the olefin moiety in 82a–b yielded the aldehydes 83a–b as a cyclization precursor, which were subjected to an intramolecular aldol cyclization with epimerization to give rise to the desired cis-fused enones 84a–b. Interestingly, the cyclization of 83a did not provide the trans-fused enone 84a, whereas the cyclization of 83b yielded a minor amount of the trans-fused enone 85b (Scheme 20).

Stereoselective introduction of alkyl groups to 84a–b from the convex face afforded the adducts 86a–e as single stereoisomers in good yields. After reduction of the ketone moiety in 86a–e, the deoxygenated products 87a–e were obtained by Barton-McCombie deoxygenation in two steps. Finally, deprotection of the methoxy carbonyl group in 87b using TMSI provided DHQ ent-cis-223F. The 1H and 13C NMR spectra of synthetic DHQ ent-cis-223F were in agreement with data from the literature [36]. In addition, by removing the methoxycarbonyl group from 87a and 87c–e, we achieved the synthesis of DHQ cis-209J, DHQ cis-251A, DHQ cis-209J-1, and DHQ cis-223F-1, respectively. Furthermore, the synthesis of DHQ cis-237U was also achieved by the treatment of DHQ ent-cis-223F with formaldehyde and NaBH3CN in MeOH (Scheme 21) [37].

Next, we investigated the synthesis of the 4a-epi-cis isomer using Weinreb amides 81a–b as a common intermediate. Treatment of 81a–b with vinylMgCl provided the vinyl ketones 88a–b, which were converted to the 4a-epi-cis enones 85a–b by the ring-closing metathesis reaction. Thereafter, the deoxygenated products 90a–b were obtained over four steps from 85a–b in the same manner as shown in Scheme 21. The NOESY experiments of 89a revealed a syn relationship between the newly incorporated methyl group at C-5 in 85a and H-8a based on the NOESY correlations from H3-5 to H-8a. Finally, removal of the methoxy carbonyl group in 90a-b gave DHQ 4a-epi-cis 195A and DHQ 4a-epi-cis 251A, respectively (Scheme 22).

Next, we investigated the synthesis of the 2-epi-cis isomer from the ester 75, which was converted to the tricyclic compound 91 via the known enaminoester 42 in several steps including the stereoselective Michael-type conjugate addition reaction, the intramolecular aldol-type cyclization reaction with epimerization, and introduction of a methyl group using a synthetic method we previously reported [23d]. Reduction of the ketone moiety in 91 followed by Barton-McCombie deoxygenation provided the reductant 92. Hydrolysis of the oxazolidinone ring in 92 provided the amino alcohol, which was treated with CbzCl to give the primary alcohol 93. Swern oxidation of 93 followed by the Wittig reaction of the resulting aldehyde afforded the olefin as a mixture of (E)- and (Z)-isomers, which was finally hydrogenated using Pearlman's catalyst to give DHQ 2-epi-cis 251A as a single isomer as shown in Scheme 23.

Finally, we examined the synthesis of the trans isomer from the homologated ester 94 prepared from 42 [23d] as shown in Scheme 24. To construct the trans-fused DHQ skeleton, cleavage of the oxazolidinone ring is essential because the ester moiety and the vinyl group of 94 are in a trans-diaxial relationship. For this purpose, hydrolysis of the oxazolidinone ring in 94 followed by treatment of the resulting carboxylic acid 95 with CH2N2 provided the corresponding ester, which was converted to the methyl urethane 96 using ClCO2Me in THF and a saturated NaHCO3 aqueous solution. Protection of the primary alcohol in 96 with MOMCl in the presence of DIPEA gave the MOM ether 97, which was transformed into the Weinreb amide 98 over two steps. Treatment of 98 with vinylMgCl followed by the ring-closing metathesis reaction of the resulting vinyl ketone 99 using a 2nd generation Grubbs catalyst afforded the trans-fused enone 100, which was subjected to the Michael-type conjugate addition reaction using Me2CuLi to afford the adducts 101a and 101b (101a: 101b=5: 1) [38]. To confirm the newly formed stereochemistry once the methyl group was introduced into 100, NOESY experiments were performed on 101a. The NOESY experiments of 101a indicated a syn relationship between the newly incorporated methyl group at C-5 in 100 and H-8a based on the NOESY correlations from H3-5 to H-8a.

The ketone moiety in 101a was reduced with NaBH4 to afford the corresponding secondary alcohol, which was converted to the deoxygenated product 102 in two steps. Deprotection of the MOM ether in 102 with TMSI provided the primary alcohol 103, which was subjected to Swern oxidation followed by the Wittig reaction of the resulting aldehyde to give rise to the mixture of (E)- and (Z)-olefin, which was then hydrogenated over 10% Pd/C to yield the trans-decahydroquinoline 104. Finally, the methoxycarbonyl group in 104 was deprotected to complete the total synthesis of DHQ trans-251A as shown in Scheme 25. With the total synthesis of the trans isomer, we achieved the divergent synthesis of DHQ-type poison-frog alkaloids, including the cis, 4a-epi-cis, and 2-epi-cis isomers from the chiral acetate 66 [39].

Our previous studies showed that several poison-frog alkaloids inhibited in vitro nicotine transport at the BBB and verapamil transport at the inner BRB [40]. The inhibition of these transport systems by DHQ cis-209J, DHQ cis-251A, DHQ cis-209J-1, DHQ cis223F1, DHQ 4a-epi-cis-195A, DHQ 4a-epi-cis-209J, DHQ 4a-epi-cis-223F, DHQ 4a-epi-cis-251A, DHQ 2-epi-cis-251A, and DHQ trans-251A was also evaluated using the model cell lines TR-BBB13 and TR-iBRB2. [3H]Nicotine uptake by TR-BBB13 cells was significantly inhibited by more than 82% in the presence of these compounds (Table 3). Moreover, decreases of [3H]verapamil uptake by TR-iBRB2 cells by at least 62% were observed in the presence of the synthesized compounds (Table 3). These results suggested that the compounds interact with nicotine-sensitive cationic drug transport mechanism(s) at the BBB and unidentified verapamil transport system(s) at the inner BRB. Because these transporters and transport mechanism(s) are involved in promotive drug transport across the BBB and inner BRB, it is expected that these compounds are distributed to the central nervous systems via specific transport mechanism(s) and/or system(s).

[3H]Nicotine uptake (0.1μCi/well, 6.0nM) by TR-BBB13 cells, an in vitro cell model of the rat BBB, was tested at 37°C for 10s in the absence (control) or presence of test compounds at 200μM with 1.0% DMSO. Similarly, [3H]verapamil uptake by TR-iBRB2 cells, an in vitro cell model of the rat inner BRB, was measured at 37°C for 3min. Each value represents the mean±standard deviation. *P<0.01, significantly different from the control evaluated by Dunnett's test.

We have achieved the divergent total synthesis of PTX- and DHQ-type poison-frog alkaloids. On the synthetic studies of PTX-type poison-frog alkaloids, PTX 209F, hPTX 223G, 8-deoxy-PTX 193H, 9-deoxy-hPTX 207O, 8-desmethyl-PTX 195, and 9-desmethyl-hPTX 209H were successfully synthesized from the common chiral building block (2R,3S)-ethyl 1-allyl-3-hydroxy-6-oxopiperidine-2-carboxylate (−)-1. In addition, the asymmetric synthesis of both enantiomers of 8-deoxy-PTX 193H and 9-deoxy-hPTX 207O were also achieved by lipase-mediated kinetic resolution of racemic (±)-4. On the synthetic studies of DHQ-type poison-frog alkaloids, we achieved the total synthesis of DHQ ent-cis-195A and DHQ cis-211A in a divergent process from the key and common intermediate enol triflate 56. The absolute stereochemistry of natural DHQ cis-211A was determined to be 2R, 4aR, 5R, 6S, and 8aS by comparison with the data obtained from our total synthesis. The inhibitory effects of DHQ ent-cis-195A, DHQ cis-211A, and DHQ 6-epi-211A on nAChRs were also investigated. The results showed that DHQ cis-211A and DHQ 6-epi-211A had better inhibitory effects on the α7-receptor than that of DHQ ent-cis-195A, and none of the compounds showed inhibitory effects on the α4β2-receptor at the same concentration. These results suggested that DHQ cis-211A and DHQ 6-epi-211A could be applied as important tools for studying the brain and nervous system. More interestingly, the absolute configuration of the DHQ nuclei of DHQ cis-211A was a mirror image of that of DHQ cis-195A, even though both alkaloids were isolated from Oophaga (Dendrobates) pumilio from Panama. Furthermore, we achieved the divergent synthesis of cis-, 4a-epi-cis-, 2-epi-cis-, and trans-DHQ-type poison-frog alkaloids from the known chiral acetate (2R,6S)-1-benzyl 2-methyl 6-(acetoxymethyl)piperidine-1,2-dicarboxylate 75 using a stereoselective Michael-type conjugate addition reaction and an intramolecular aldol-type cyclization with epimerization. Through the above synthetic studies, we were able to establish that chiral building blocks (−)-1 and 75 are extremely useful and versatile for the synthesis of natural products, especially indolizidine, quinolizidine, and decahydroquinoline alkaloids.
